europa: The European Council sets the EU's political direction. The Council of the EU co-legislates, co-decides the budget and decides foreign and tax policy, often by unanimity.
berlaymont: Holds the near-exclusive right to propose EU laws, enforces them, runs competition and trade policy and executes the budget.
nato: Political headquarters of a 32-member alliance whose collective defence commitment underpins European security.
ep: Co-legislator with the Council on most laws, co-decides the budget, elects the Commission President and can censure the Commission.
justus: Where COREPER and the Council's preparatory bodies negotiate member-state positions before ministers sign off.
charlemagne: DG Trade negotiates every EU trade agreement and runs trade defence on behalf of all 27 member states.
beaulieu: DG CONNECT drafts the EU's digital rulebook and supervises the largest online platforms under the Digital Services Act.
eeas: Runs EU diplomacy and prepares sanctions, but foreign-policy decisions need member states' unanimity.
usmission: Represents the EU's largest trade and security partner. Influence comes from leverage, not a seat at the table.
edps: Can order EU institutions to change how they process personal data and take them to the Court of Justice.
eda: Coordinates joint defence projects, while member states keep control of procurement.
ukmission: A third country since Brexit, the UK now shapes EU policy through negotiation rather than votes.
delors: The Economic and Social Committee and Committee of the Regions must be consulted on many laws, but their opinions are advisory.
covent: Executive agencies hand out research and innovation grants under rules set elsewhere.

PLACES.d: Headquarters of the European Commission. The College of Commissioners meets on the 13th floor, usually on Wednesdays, and most EU legislation starts life here as a Commission proposal.
Commission building that houses DG Trade, the team that negotiates the EU's trade agreements on behalf of all member states.
The Council's working building. National diplomats meet here in working parties and in COREPER, the committee of ambassadors that prepares nearly every ministerial decision.
Seat of the European Council and the Council of the EU since 2017. Leaders hold summits here and ministers formally adopt EU laws.
Parliament's Brussels home: committees, political groups and shorter plenary sessions meet here. The twelve main plenary sessions each year take place in Strasbourg.
Parliament's free visitor centre, with an interactive introduction to how the EU works.
Museum opened by Parliament in 2017 in Parc Léopold, covering European history from the 19th century onward.
Home of the European Economic and Social Committee and the European Committee of the Regions, which give formal opinions on draft laws.
The EU's diplomatic service, led by the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
Commission offices in Auderghem that house DG CONNECT, the department behind the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act and the AI Act.
A 34-storey tower used by the Commission, one of many office blocks the institution rents across the city.
Independent authority that supervises how EU institutions themselves handle personal data.
Office tower near Gare du Nord housing several EU executive agencies that manage research and innovation funding.
Political headquarters of the Alliance, opened on this site in 2017. The North Atlantic Council, NATO's main decision-making body, meets here.
EU agency, founded in 2004, that helps member states develop military capabilities together and coordinate defence procurement.
Since Brexit, the UK is represented here as a third country rather than as a member state.
Washington's diplomatic mission to the European Union, separate from the US embassy to Belgium.
Launched in 2015, its morning newsletters are standard reading across the EU quarter.
EU policy news outlet with sections on each major policy area.
A 1920s apartment complex turned International Press Centre, home to many foreign correspondents' bureaux.
Venue for press conferences and briefings, used by NGOs, governments and companies alike.
Seat of Belgium's Federal Parliament. The Prime Minister's office is next door.
The King's official workplace, facing the Palace of the Nation across Brussels Park.
Parliament of the Brussels-Capital Region, responsible for planning, housing, mobility and the environment in the city.
'Plux' to locals. On Thursday evenings the square fills with parliamentary assistants, lobbyists and journalists for after-work drinks.
Irish pub by the Berlaymont, a long-standing meeting spot for the Commission crowd.
Square with Maison Antoine, the frites stand that every EU official seems to have an opinion about.
Green space tucked behind Parliament, a lunchtime refuge with a pond and old science buildings.
Monumental park at the end of Rue de la Loi, built for Belgium's 50th anniversary in 1880.
Metro and rail hub under the roundabout at the heart of the EU quarter, with direct trains to the airport.
Rail station built partly beneath the Parliament complex.
Station in the EU quarter where 16 people were killed in the terrorist attack of 22 March 2016. A memorial now lines the platforms.
International rail hub for Eurostar to London and Paris, and high-speed trains to Amsterdam and Germany.
About 20 minutes by train from Schuman.

businesseurope: The confederation of national employers' federations and the organisation with the most top-level Commission meetings this term.
amcham: Represents American companies investing in Europe.
digitaleurope: Trade association of the digital technology industry, active on AI, data and platform regulation.
etuc: Umbrella body for national trade unions and the official voice of workers in EU social dialogue.
copa: Represents European farmers, a powerful voice on the Common Agricultural Policy.
tieu: Tracks lobbying and integrity in the EU institutions.
ceo: Research and campaign group that investigates corporate lobbying in Brussels.
bruegel: Economics think tank founded in 2005, influential on competition, trade, energy and fiscal policy.
ceps: The Centre for European Policy Studies, one of Brussels' oldest EU-focused think tanks.
epc: Think tank working on EU integration, migration, social policy and Europe's place in the world.
carnegie: European centre of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
friends: Think tank known for debates bringing together policymakers, business and civil society.
egmont: Belgium's Royal Institute for International Relations.

STORIES.title: How an EU law travels
STORIES.intro: Follow a typical piece of EU legislation from first draft to final adoption, a journey of about a kilometre that often takes two years.

steps.t: The Commission drafts a proposal. For most EU laws, it alone has the right to propose.
Advisory committees representing employers, unions, civil society and regions give their opinions.
A Parliament committee names a rapporteur, amends the text and Parliament adopts its position, usually in a Strasbourg plenary.
In parallel, national diplomats in Council working parties and COREPER build the member states' position.
Trilogues: Parliament, Council and Commission negotiate a compromise behind closed doors, in Parliament or Council buildings.
Ministers formally adopt the agreed text. It's published in the Official Journal and becomes law.

STORIES.title: The influence circuit
STORIES.intro: A short walk through the organisations with the most access to the Commission, and the people who watch them.

steps.t: More top-level Commission meetings this term than any other registered organisation.
American companies coordinate their positions on EU rules.
The tech industry lobbies on AI, data and platform regulation.
Consumer groups make the counter-case, often on the same files.
Watchdogs track who meets whom through the EU Transparency Register.
Thursday night: the deals, gossip and job offers that happen outside office hours.

STORIES.title: The Council's engine room
STORIES.intro: Member states negotiate through their permanent representations. The biggest hold the most weight in qualified-majority votes, but every one can block a unanimity file.

steps.t: Germany carries the largest share of the EU population, and so the most weight under qualified majority voting.
France, the second-largest vote, and a frequent co-author of compromises with Berlin.
Poland, the largest of the 2004 entrants.
Malta, the smallest member state, with the same veto as Germany on unanimity files.
Ambassadors meet in COREPER to settle what ministers will sign off.

STORIES.title: Security Brussels
STORIES.intro: Brussels is also the capital of Western defence diplomacy, from NATO's Evere campus to the EU's own foreign service.

steps.t: Allies decide by consensus in the North Atlantic Council.
The EU's foreign service runs sanctions, diplomacy and civilian missions.
Member states plan joint defence capabilities and procurement.
Washington's line into EU foreign and trade policy.
Belgium's foreign policy think tank, where many of these debates get aired.
